subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

tasks_in_class.description: Given 35÷1=___, write the corresponding multiplication fact and two division facts that follow.
Identify numbers to fill circles so that square values are the products or quotients of the circle numbers in a multiplication-division web.
Solve four multiplication problems (30×30, 400×8, 15×60, 200×16) and write two division statements for each.

time_bands.activity: Draw a 5-by-7 dot array on the board; ask children how many dots in all, then invite them to write the multiplication fact. Record 5×7=35 and 7×5=35, then ask: if you know the total and one side, how do you find the other? Collect two or three verbal answers and write the pair 35÷5=7 and 35÷7=5 beside the array. Establish that N=D×Q means the dividend equals the divisor times the quotient.

Think and answer, p.119 ("Given 35÷1=___, write the corresponding multiplication fact...."). Children work individually; one or two share, and the class checks each answer against the array idea: multiply divisor by quotient to recover 35.

Let Us Play, p.120 ("Identify numbers to fill circles so that square values are the products...."). Pairs complete the multiplication-division web; bring the class together to compare choices and notice each correct placement satisfies both a multiplication and a division fact simultaneously.

Let Us Do Q1, p.120 ("Solve four multiplication problems (30×30, 400×8, 15×60, 200×16)...."). Children work the four products then write the two division facts each yields; teacher circulates and listens for children who reverse divisor and dividend, prompting them to re-read the array idea.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often believe division is a separate, harder operation rather than the reverse of multiplication; grounding each division sentence in the coconut-array image (N=D×Q) helps correct this. Watch for children who write only one division fact per multiplication — pause and ask whether swapping divisor and quotient still checks out. The web activity works well in pairs so children can talk through each circle and square placement aloud.
materials: Squared paper or dot-grid sheets for arrays

section_titles: Patterns in division and place value
periods.activity_title: Scaling Up: What Happens to Quotients?

tasks_in_class.description: Solve 18 division problems arranged in scaling patterns; fill two place value (H–T–O) charts and discuss what happens to quotients in each case.

time_bands.activity: Write the triplet 150÷3, 1500÷3, 15000÷3 on the board without answers. Ask children to guess the quotients in order, then share with a partner. Draw a blank H–T–O chart and fill it with 150, showing which digit sits in which column; repeat for 1500 extended to Th–H–T–O. Establish that annexing a zero shifts every digit one place left, so the quotient too grows by a factor of ten.

Let Us Do Q2, p.121 ("Solve 18 division problems arranged in scaling patterns; fill two place value (H–T–O) charts...."). Children work in groups of three: one child solves, one records in the place value chart, one watches for the pattern and announces it. Rotate roles for each set of three problems. Circulate and probe: 'What stays the same? What changes?'

Groups share one pattern each; teacher records the generalisations on the board (e.g. 'dividing the divisor by 10 multiplies the quotient by 10'). Children copy the two confirmed generalisations into their notebooks in their own words, then test each with one new example they invent themselves.

Quick oral round: teacher reads a dividend–divisor pair (e.g. 2000÷20) and children hold up their slates or write the quotient on paper. Use responses to surface any remaining confusion between scaling dividend and scaling divisor before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse 'multiply the dividend by 10' with 'multiply the divisor by 10' and expect the quotient to behave the same way both times; the place value chart makes the opposite effect visible. Encourage children to articulate the pattern in words before writing any symbols — verbal generalisation before symbolic recording is the key step here. The group rotation (solve–record–observe) keeps all three children active and surfaces the pattern through discussion rather than instruction.
materials: Blank H–T–O chart strips (one per group)
Slates or small whiteboards for the oral round

section_titles: Patterns in division and place value
periods.activity_title: Scaling Division — Story Problems and Puzzles

tasks_in_class.description: Sabina cycles 160 km in 20 days. How many kilometres does she cycle each day?
How many ₹100 notes does Seema need to buy coconuts worth ₹4200?
₹5500 distributed equally among 5 employees; what if distributed among 10? Will each get more or less? How much would be needed to give all the same amount?
Place numbers 1–8 in boxes so all four operations (÷, ×, +, −) are correct with no repetition.

homework.description: Fill in 8 blanks (a–h) using the relationship N=D×Q (e.g. ___÷18=100, 870÷___=87).

time_bands.activity: Pose the Sabina problem verbally before the books open: 'She travels 160 km in 20 days — how far each day?' Children estimate first (is it closer to 5, 8, or 15?), then confirm with division. Link to the scaling pattern built earlier: 160÷20 = 16÷2 scaled.

Let Us Do Q1, p.122 ("Sabina cycles 160 km in 20 days. How many kilometres does she cycle each day?") and Let Us Do Q2, p.122 ("How many ₹100 notes does Seema need to buy coconuts worth ₹4200?"). Children work individually, writing a division sentence before computing. Pairs compare and resolve differences.

Let Us Do Q3, p.122 ("₹5500 distributed equally among 5 employees; what if distributed among 10?...."). Children discuss in pairs: will each person's share increase or decrease, and why? One pair shares their reasoning; class checks with the calculation, then answers the third part about keeping shares equal.

Let Us Do Q4, p.122 ("Place numbers 1–8 in boxes so all four operations (÷, ×, +, −) are correct with no repetition."). Children work individually, then compare solutions with a neighbour. Teacher notes that more than one arrangement may be possible and invites any child who found a different solution to share it.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes set up Q3 as a subtraction (5500−10) rather than recognising it as a division-scaling situation; redirecting them to write the division sentence first usually resolves this. The four-operations placement puzzle in Q4 benefits from a try-and-adjust approach — reassure children that crossing out and retrying is part of mathematical thinking, not a mistake. Let Us Do Q5, p.122, which practises using N=D×Q to find missing dividends or divisors, is set for home practice to consolidate the relationship at a comfortable pace.

periods.activity_title: Split It or Halve It: Mental Division Strategies

tasks_in_class.description: Apply splitting and/or repeated halving strategies to solve: 64÷4, 265÷5, 1560÷8, 4824÷24, 168÷8, 144÷4 using scaffolded diagram frames.

time_bands.activity: Write 1248÷6 on the board. Ask: 'Is there a part of 1248 you can divide by 6 easily?' Elicit 1200 (200 sixes) and 48 (8 sixes). Record 1248÷6 = 1200÷6 + 48÷6 = 200+8 = 208. Now try 1992÷4 together: children suggest rounding up to 2000 and subtracting 8÷4. Establish the two strategies — additive splitting and subtractive splitting — in words on the board. Then demonstrate repeated halving: 128÷4, halve to 64, halve again to 32.

Try It! Q1–6, p.123 ("Apply splitting and/or repeated halving strategies to solve: 64÷4, 265÷5, 1560÷8, 4824÷24, 168÷8, 144÷4...."). Children use the scaffolded frames in the book; they choose which strategy to apply, then note their choice beside each answer. Teacher circulates, asking 'Why did you split there?' or 'Could you halve instead?'

Compare strategies: ask which problems were quicker to halve and which were easier to split. Children who chose different strategies for the same problem share their working. Record one 'split' solution and one 'halve' solution for the same dividend side by side to show both reach the same answer.
Children write one division of their own (dividend between 100 and 2000, divisor 2, 4, 5, or 8) and solve it using the strategy they found more comfortable, then swap with a neighbour to verify.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is an uneven split — children split 1248 into 1000 and 248 when 1200 and 48 is far cleaner; prompting 'What multiple of your divisor is close to 1248?' redirects them. Repeated halving works only when the divisor is a power of 2; children sometimes try to halve for divisors like 5 or 6, so a quick group check of 'Will halving work here?' prevents this. Encourage children to generate their own examples in the closing minutes, as the act of composing a problem deepens understanding of when each strategy applies.

section_titles: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
periods.activity_title: Susie's Method: Building Quotients Step by Step

tasks_in_class.description: Solve eight division problems using partial quotient strategies: 256÷4, 545÷5, 147÷7, 1212÷6, 648÷12, 9648÷48, 775÷25, 796÷4.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Susie's method on the board using a fresh example — say 168÷6. Ask: 'How many sixes fit in 168? Let's subtract a batch we are sure of.' Record 6×10=60, subtract to get 108; then 6×10=60, subtract to get 48; then 6×8=48, subtract to get 0. Add partial quotients: 10+10+8=28. Verify: 6×28=168. Repeat for a second example (say 195÷5) inviting children to suggest each batch. Introduce Sunitha's refinement: choose a larger initial batch (6×20=120) to reduce steps, reaching the same answer faster. Write the relationship N=D×Q+R and show how remainder arises when the final subtraction leaves a non-zero value.

Let Us Solve (a–h), p.124 ("Solve eight division problems using partial quotient strategies: 256÷4, 545÷5, 147÷7, 1212÷6, 648÷12, 9648÷48, 775÷25, 796÷4."). Children work individually on the first four, then pairs for the last four. After each answer children write the check: D×Q+R=N.

Gallery-style: two children write their working for 775÷25 on the board — one using many small batches, one using fewer large batches. Class identifies which is Susie's style and which is Sunitha's, and discusses which required fewer steps without declaring one method superior.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes subtract an over-sized batch and reach a negative remainder; reminding them 'subtract only what you are sure fits' and modelling 'is 6×20 ≤ 108?' before each step prevents this. The verification step N=D×Q+R is not optional — insist children write it for every problem, as it is the internal self-check that builds the habit. The two-child board comparison in the closing minutes makes Sunitha's efficiency advantage concrete without dismissing Susie's method.

section_titles: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
periods.activity_title: Coconut Farm Word Problems and Scaffold Frames

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Susie's Farm in Kerala Q1, p.124
tasks_in_class.description: 582 coconuts sold equally to 6 customers; how many each? How many bags of 25 needed for 97 coconuts? Discuss which method (Susie's or Sunitha's) is better.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let Us Learn to Divide, p.125
tasks_in_class.description: Complete scaffolded partial-quotient frames for 726÷4 and 902÷16; verify using N=D×Q+R and check whether 726=4×181 and 902=16×56.

time_bands.activity: Susie's Farm in Kerala Q1, p.124 ("582 coconuts sold equally to 6 customers; how many each?...."). Children read the problem silently, then write one sentence naming the operation and the numbers. They solve using whichever partial-quotient style they prefer, then answer the bags question (97÷25, noting the remainder means one extra bag is needed). Pairs discuss: did you use Susie's step-by-step or Sunitha's larger-batch approach, and why?

Let Us Learn to Divide, p.125 ("Complete scaffolded partial-quotient frames for 726÷4 and 902÷16; verify using N=D×Q+R...."). Children fill the frames independently, then check: does 4×181 = 724 with remainder 2, making 726? Does 16×56 = 896 with remainder 6, making 902? Children who arrive at a different quotient trace back through their subtraction steps to find the slip.

Pair-share: each child tells their partner one thing they noticed while verifying — a step where they over-subtracted, a useful batch size, or when the remainder was bigger than the divisor and needed an extra step. One pair shares with the class; teacher records the key observation on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The bags problem (97÷25) introduces the practical interpretation of a remainder — you need one extra bag for the leftover coconuts — which children often miss by simply ignoring the remainder. Stress that the verification 4×181+2=726 must be written, not guessed; scaffold frames that arrive at a wrong quotient are very common when children drop a partial-quotient batch. The inquiry in the scaffold frame task works best when children are encouraged to ask 'Is my remainder smaller than the divisor?' after each subtraction step rather than at the end.

section_titles: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
periods.activity_title: Multi-Step Word Problems on the Coconut Farm

tasks_in_class.description: Word problems: oil from 4376 coconuts (4376÷8); theatre samosa packs; buses for 342 students; Sofia's note combinations; picnic cost split; check N=D×Q+R for six division problems (a–f).

time_bands.activity: Warm-up: display 4376÷8 and ask children to estimate the quotient by rounding 4376 to 4400 or 4000. Record two or three estimates; note whose is closest. This builds the habit of predicting before computing.

Let Us Solve Q1–5, p.126 ("Word problems: oil from 4376 coconuts; theatre samosa packs; buses for 342 students; Sofia's note combinations; picnic cost split...."). Children work in pairs: one sets up the division sentence, the other computes using any partial-quotient style. They swap roles for each new problem. After every answer both children write the N=D×Q+R check.

Let Us Solve Q1–5, p.126 (part b — check N=D×Q+R for six division problems (a–f)). Children examine six ready-computed divisions and verify each. If a verification fails, they identify whether the error is in the quotient or the remainder, then correct it.
Exit reflection: each child writes one sentence — 'The hardest part was ___ because ___.' Teacher collects to inform the next unit's opening.

periods.teacher_notes: The buses problem (342 students) is a classic remainder-interpretation question — the remainder means one extra bus is needed, and children who write the answer as a decimal or ignore the remainder will arrive at an incorrect real-world answer. Sofia's note combinations problem may require more than one operation; encourage children to break it into steps rather than trying to solve in a single division. The verification round at the end of this unit is deliberate: catching a wrong quotient by checking is more transferable than being told the right answer.

periods.activity_title: Distributing by Place: Hundreds, Then Tens, Then Ones

tasks_in_class.description: Complete four division problems (7032÷6, 3005÷5, 2874÷14, 9805÷32) using both partial quotient scaffold and place-value (Th–H–T–O) algorithm side by side.

time_bands.activity: Model the place-value algorithm on the board using 324÷3. Draw a Th–H–T–O column chart beside the long-division frame. Distribute: 3 Hundreds ÷ 3 = 1 Hundred; 2 Tens ÷ 3 — not enough, regroup 2 Tens = 20 Ones plus 4 = 24 Ones; 24÷3 = 8. Show quotient 108. Ask: 'Where does the zero come from?' (no tens fit). Repeat with 62÷5 to show the two-digit version, placing the zero explicitly. Children copy both worked examples and annotate the regrouping arrows.

Let Us Divide (a–d), p.130–131 ("Complete four division problems (7032÷6, 3005÷5, 2874÷14, 9805÷32) using both partial quotient scaffold and place-value (Th–H–T–O) algorithm side by side."). Children complete both columns for each problem. The partial-quotient column gives an independent check on the place-value column answer.

Pair comparison: partners check each other's place-value column answers by running the partial-quotient answer through N=D×Q+R. Any mismatch triggers a joint review of the regrouping step where the slip occurred.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in the place-value algorithm is omitting the zero in the quotient when a digit cannot be divided — children jump to the next digit without recording the zero, producing a quotient that is a factor of ten too small. Insisting that every place-value position has a digit (including zero) in the quotient row before moving on catches this. The side-by-side comparison with partial quotients is the key scaffolding here: children who get different answers in the two columns know immediately that one contains an error, without needing teacher confirmation.

periods.activity_title: Finding What's Missing: Divisors, Dividends and Riddles

tasks_in_class.description: Find missing divisors or dividends in 10 scaffolded division frames so there is no remainder; solve riddle: 3-digit number ÷5=42 and ×2=420.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: '___÷6=12'. Ask children to work backwards — if Q=12 and D=6, what is N? Record N=D×Q=72. Now try '54÷___=9'. Children identify D=6 by dividing N by Q. Establish the two inverse moves: to find N multiply D×Q; to find D divide N by Q. Work one more example together — '___÷9=11' — before the book task opens.

Let Us Do Q1, p.131 ("Find missing divisors or dividends in 10 scaffolded division frames so there is no remainder; solve riddle...."). Children work individually on the 10 frames, then tackle the riddle (3-digit number ÷5=42 and ×2=420). Circulate and ask children who find the riddle difficult: 'If ÷5 gives 42, what do you multiply by 5 to check?'

Three children place their riddle solutions on the board (possibly arriving at different 3-digit numbers if they misread the clue). Class checks each against both conditions: does the number ÷5=42? Does the number ×2=420? Precisely one number satisfies both; children agree on why the other attempts fail.
Children write one missing-value problem of their own (give N and Q, leave D blank) and swap with a neighbour to solve in the remaining moments.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who attempt the riddle by trial and error rather than reasoning from ÷5=42 will often find a number satisfying one condition but not both; guide them to use the multiplication inverse first (42×5=210) before checking the second condition. The 10 scaffold frames vary in whether N or D is missing, so a quick class sort ('Which frames give you N? Which give you D?') before independent work helps children choose the right inverse move. Composing their own missing-value problem in the closing minutes is a metacognitive check — a child who cannot compose one does not yet fully own the relationship.

periods.activity_title: Word Problems, Patterns and Missing Information

tasks_in_class.description: Word problems: theatre shows for 475 people; ice cream per friend; biscuits per person per day; six division problems with remainder check; pattern sets A/B/C; cycle rally distance; identify missing information in 4 problems; bookshelf resource constraint problem.
Complete Munshi Lal's erased record book: find missing total amounts, quantities, and cost per kg for 4 vegetables using multiplication and division.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1–8, p.132–133 ("Word problems: theatre shows for 475 people; ice cream per friend; biscuits per person per day; six division problems with remainder check; pattern sets A/B/C; cycle rally distance; identify missing information in 4 problems; bookshelf resource constraint problem."). Children work individually; teacher pauses the class at the missing-information problems to ask: 'Before you divide, do you have all the numbers you need?' and at the bookshelf problem to ask: 'Which resource runs out first?'

Vegetable Market table, p.134 ("Complete Munshi Lal's erased record book: find missing total amounts, quantities, and cost per kg for 4 vegetables...."). Children identify for each row whether the missing cell requires multiplication or division, write the operation, then compute. Pairs compare rows and resolve differences.

Whole-class share of the bookshelf resource constraint problem: invite two children to explain how they identified the binding constraint. Record the key reasoning step on the board: divide each stock by its requirement, then take the smallest quotient.

periods.teacher_notes: The missing-information problems are designed to break the habit of computing before reading carefully — children who dive into arithmetic on problems that lack a necessary number will hit a wall; that productive frustration is the teaching point, not a sign to rescue them immediately. The Vegetable Market table requires children to move between multiplication and division within the same table, and children often try to apply one operation to every row; having them label each cell 'need ×' or 'need ÷' before computing is a useful pre-step. The bookshelf problem extends into multi-step reasoning and can be left as a stretch for early finishers if time is tight.

periods.activity_title: Fluency with the Place-Value Algorithm: 12 Problems

time_bands.activity: Children sort the 12 problems into two groups before computing: those with a 1-digit divisor and those with a 2-digit divisor. Ask: 'Does the number of steps differ? Will the algorithm change?' Establish that the place-value distribution process is the same — more places, same logic.

Let Us Solve Q1–12, p.134 ("Divide 12 problems (506÷5, 918÷8, 8126÷7, 9324÷4, 876÷6, 7008÷3, 934÷12, 829÷23, 705÷18, 8704÷32, 6790÷45, 5074÷21) using place value; identify remainder; check N=D×Q+R."). Children work independently; after every four problems they pause and verify using N=D×Q+R before continuing.

Children self-mark by comparing with a partner; for any disagreement they trace through the place-value column step by step to find where the values diverge. Teacher targets any child who has multiple mismatches for a one-to-one step-through of one problem.

Children identify which of the 12 problems produced a non-zero remainder and write the full check for those; they note whether any remainder equals or exceeds the divisor (which would mean the quotient needs one more step).

periods.teacher_notes: Seven-thousand-eight divided by three (7008÷3) and 3005÷5 from the previous unit are the canonical zero-in-the-middle problems; children who skip a place-value position without recording zero will get a quotient an order of magnitude too small and the verification will immediately expose this. The verification-every-four-problems rhythm is deliberate — catching errors early prevents children from building 12 wrong answers before any feedback. A remainder that equals or exceeds the divisor signals an incomplete division, not a valid remainder, and is worth highlighting explicitly.

section_titles: Mathematical statements and reasoning about operations
periods.activity_title: Always, Sometimes, Never: Reasoning About Arithmetic

tasks_in_class.description: Complete 4 statements to make them true: 7×6=___+17; 87+6=___×31; 63+___=74−4; ___÷9=16÷2.
Find 5 examples for 'odd+odd=even'; find examples or counterexamples for '×2 gives odd'; give 3 examples and 3 counterexamples for 'halving always gives even'.
Tick Always/Sometimes/Never for 5 statements about adding 10, subtraction order, doubling-halving in multiplication, odd×n=even, and multiplying by 5.

time_bands.activity: Mathematical Statements Q1, p.135 ("Determine True or False for 5 equations: 8×9=70+2; 20−6=7×3; 48÷3=4×4; 89−9=90+0; 25+10=45−10."). Children evaluate each side independently, then compare. Stress that both sides must be computed — the equals sign is a balance, not an instruction to write the answer on the right.

Mathematical Statements Q2, p.135 ("Complete 4 statements to make them true: 7×6=___+17; 87+6=___×31; 63+___=74−4; ___÷9=16÷2."). Children work individually; when they finish, one child writes their answer for 87+6=___×31 on the board and the class checks it together.

Mathematical Statements Q3, p.135 ("Find 5 examples for 'odd+odd=even'; find examples or counterexamples for '×2 gives odd'; give 3 examples and 3 counterexamples for 'halving always gives even'...."). Pairs generate examples; once one counterexample to '×2 gives odd' is found, the class discusses whether one counterexample is enough to disprove a 'always' claim.

Mathematical Statements Q4, p.135 ("Tick Always/Sometimes/Never for 5 statements about adding 10, subtraction order, doubling-halving in multiplication, odd×n=even, and multiplying by 5."). Children work individually, then compare with a partner; pairs who disagree on a tick must produce either an example (for Sometimes or Always) or a counterexample (for Never or Sometimes) to settle the dispute.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often interpret the equals sign as 'write the answer here' rather than as a balance between two equal quantities; the True/False task in Q1 is an effective corrective because computing both sides forces the balance reading. The key mathematical idea in Q3 and Q4 is that one counterexample is sufficient to refute an 'always' claim but any number of examples cannot prove it — introduce this logic gently using 'odd+odd=even' as the case where no counterexample exists. The 'halving always gives even' statement in Q3 is a classic trap: halving an odd number does not give a whole number at all, which may surprise children and leads to a productive discussion about the domain of the claim.

section_titles: Patterns in division and place value
Long division using partial quotients and remainder
Mathematical statements and reasoning about operations
periods.activity_title: Coconut Farm: Connecting Every Strand of Division

time_bands.activity: Open with a class-wide challenge: write 4824÷24 on the board. Children choose any method they know — mental splitting, repeated halving, partial quotients, or the place-value algorithm — and solve it independently. Three children share their working, naming the method they used. Class verifies each using N=D×Q+R and confirms all three (if correct) reach the same quotient, establishing that multiple valid paths exist.

Pose three rapid-fire oral questions connecting the chapter's threads: (1) 'I know 7×8=56. Without dividing, write two division facts.' (2) '3000÷30 — what does scaling the divisor by 10 do to the quotient, and why?' (3) 'Is odd×odd always odd? Give an example and say whether you are proving or only supporting the claim.' Children write answers, then pairs compare and discuss the third question's distinction between example and proof.

Coconut farm scenario: 'Sunitha has 9805 coconuts. She packs them equally into crates of 32. How many full crates? How many coconuts are left over?' Children solve using the place-value algorithm, write the full N=D×Q+R check, then answer: 'If she now distributes the leftover coconuts equally among 5 workers, how many does each receive, and are there any remaining?' Children present the two-step solution in their notebooks, showing both division computations and both verification checks.

Mathematical statements round: teacher reads two statements — 'Dividing a number by 10 always gives a whole number' and 'Multiplying by 2 then dividing by 2 always returns the original number.' Children tick Always / Sometimes / Never, then produce either an example and a counterexample (Sometimes) or a counterexample alone (Never). Pairs discuss why one counterexample settles a 'Never' claim while the 'Always' claim about multiplying then dividing needs a reason, not just examples.

Exit card: each child writes one sentence completing 'Division and multiplication are connected because ___', drawing on any concept from the chapter — inverse relationship, N=D×Q+R, scaling patterns, or the verification step — to close the chapter on their own terms.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit deliberately revisits every strand — multiplication-division inverse (the exit card), scaling patterns (the oral question on 3000÷30), mental strategies (the opening 4824÷24 comparison), partial quotients and the place-value algorithm (the coconut farm scenario), and always-sometimes-never reasoning (the statements round). Where children choose different methods for the opening problem, accept all correct solutions and use the agreement of answers as the chapter's culminating point: the algorithm is a tool, not the mathematics itself. The exit card sentence is open-ended by design — there is no single correct phrasing, and a child who writes something unexpected is worth a one-to-one conversation.
materials: Board for the opening challenge and oral questions
Exit card slips or a notebook page

items.section_title: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
items.prompt: Use the partial quotient method to divide 852 by 4. Show each step by subtracting one batch at a time. After you find the quotient and remainder, write the check: 4 × quotient + remainder = 852.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract known multiples of the divisor step by step and add the partial quotients.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student begin with small batches (4×10) and build up; stretch: ask them to reach the answer in two steps instead of three.

exercise.book_ref: Let Us Learn to Divide, p.125
exercise.description: Complete scaffolded partial-quotient frames for 726÷4 and 902÷16; verify using N=D×Q+R and check whether 726=4×181 and 902=16×56.

items.prompt: Meena knows that 9 × 6 = 54. Without doing any new multiplication, write two different division facts that follow directly from this. Explain in one sentence why both facts are true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 54 ÷ 9 = 6 and 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Both are true because the dividend (54) equals the divisor multiplied by the quotient, so swapping divisor and quotient gives a second valid division.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the inverse relationship: if D × Q = N, then N ÷ D = Q and N ÷ Q = D.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 9-by-6 array and ask how many rows and how many in each row; stretch: ask the student to write the two division facts for 8×7 and then for 12×9 without any array.

exercise.description: Identify numbers to fill circles so that square values are the products or quotients of the circle numbers in a multiplication-division web.

items.section_title: Patterns in division and place value
items.prompt: Rajan knows that 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Which of the following is the correct value of 2400 ÷ 3?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiplying the dividend by 100 multiplies the quotient by 100, so 8 × 100 = 800.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ignored the scaling entirely and used the basic fact without adjustment.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student scaled by 10 instead of 100, confusing 2400 with 240.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-scaled by 1000, possibly counting three zeros in 2400 rather than seeing it as 24 × 100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 24 and 2400 in a H–T–O chart side by side and ask which column the 24 sits in each; stretch: ask what 24000 ÷ 3 would be and why.

exercise.description: Solve 18 division problems arranged in scaling patterns; fill two place value (H–T–O) charts and discuss what happens to quotients in each case.

items.section_title: Patterns in division and place value
items.prompt: ₹6000 is shared equally among 6 workers. A second group of 12 workers also wants the same total amount split equally. Will each person in the second group get more or less than each person in the first group? Write the two division calculations and explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: First group: 6000 ÷ 6 = 1000 each. Second group needs 6000 ÷ 12 = 500 each. Each person in the second group gets less (₹500 vs ₹1000) because doubling the number of people halves each share.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Doubling the divisor halves the quotient when the dividend stays the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 6 boxes and share 6000 dots in tens, then redraw with 12 boxes; stretch: ask how many workers would each receive ₹250 from the same total.

exercise.description: ₹5500 distributed equally among 5 employees; what if distributed among 10? Will each get more or less? How much would be needed to give all the same amount?

items.section_title: Patterns in division and place value
items.prompt:
Place the numbers 2, 3, 6, and 9 into the four boxes below so that both number sentences are correct at the same time. You may use each number only once.

___ ÷ ___ = ___
___ × ___ = ___

(Use the same four numbers across both sentences.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid arrangement: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 2 × 3 = 6, using 6, 3, 2 across both. Another: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 is not valid (repetition). A clean solution using all four: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 3 × 3 = 9 — but 3 appears twice. Fully non-repeating with all four: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 for the division (uses 6, 3, 2) and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 is repeated; accept 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and separately 9 ÷ 3 = 3 as two valid division facts from the set. The clearest non-repeating pair: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 (division) and 2 × 3 = 6 (multiplication), treating each sentence as its own complete use of its numbers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the inverse relationship: a multiplication fact yields a corresponding division fact with the same three numbers.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: begin with any multiplication fact using two of the four numbers and ask what division fact follows; stretch: find a second completely different arrangement using the same four numbers.

exercise.description: Place numbers 1–8 in boxes so all four operations (÷, ×, +, −) are correct with no repetition.

items.prompt: A number divided by 7 gives a quotient of 105 with no remainder. What is that number?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: To find a missing dividend with no remainder, multiply divisor by quotient: N = D × Q.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student wrote 7 and 105 side by side, ignoring the multiplication, producing 705.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student estimated loosely (700 + 50) without computing the product.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student made an arithmetic slip in 7 × 105, likely computing 7 × 100 + 7 × 3 = 721 and rounding.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write N = D × Q and ask the student to substitute D=7 and Q=105 before multiplying; stretch: ask what the number would be if the quotient were 105 remainder 4.

exercise.description: Find missing divisors or dividends in 10 scaffolded division frames so there is no remainder; solve riddle: 3-digit number ÷5=42 and ×2=420.

items.section_title: Mathematical statements and reasoning about operations
items.prompt: A friend says: 'Multiplying any number by 2 always gives an even result.' Find 3 examples that support this statement. Then explain whether examples alone are enough to prove it is always true, or whether one counterexample would be enough to prove it is never true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Examples such as 3×2=6, 7×2=14, 15×2=30 support the statement. Examples alone cannot prove it is always true for every possible number. However, one counterexample would be enough to disprove an 'always' claim — but in this case none exists, because any whole number times 2 ends in an even digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test with examples to support and look for a counterexample to disprove; a single counterexample refutes an 'always' claim.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try only odd numbers ×2 and record whether the result is odd or even; stretch: ask whether the statement still holds if the number is very large (e.g. 1001×2) and why.

exercise.description: Find 5 examples for 'odd+odd=even'; find examples or counterexamples for '×2 gives odd'; give 3 examples and 3 counterexamples for 'halving always gives even'.

items.section_title: Mathematical statements and reasoning about operations
items.prompt: Which label correctly describes the statement: 'Adding 10 to any number gives a number that ends in 0'?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sometimes true. Adding 10 to 20 gives 30 (ends in 0), but adding 10 to 23 gives 33 (does not end in 0). It is true only when the original number ends in 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test with one example that ends in 0 (supports) and one that does not (counterexample), then classify.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student tested only numbers ending in 0 and assumed the pattern holds for all numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focused only on cases where the result does not end in 0 and dismissed the valid cases.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused 'ending in 0' with 'even', not realising even numbers can end in 2, 4, 6, or 8.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: try adding 10 to 30, then to 37, and compare the last digits; stretch: write one more statement of your own and decide its label with an example and a counterexample.

exercise.description: Tick Always/Sometimes/Never for 5 statements about adding 10, subtraction order, doubling-halving in multiplication, odd×n=even, and multiplying by 5.

items.prompt: Which pair of division facts follows directly from 8 × 9 = 72?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: From D × Q = N, write N ÷ D = Q and N ÷ Q = D using the same three numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student kept one fact correct but replaced 72 with 80 in the second, showing the dividend is not fixed in their understanding.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student swapped quotients, assigning each divisor its own value rather than the other's.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student replaced one factor (8) with a nearby number (7), showing a recall slip rather than a conceptual error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw an 8-by-9 grid and ask how many in each row and each column; stretch: write the two division facts for 12 × 11 = 132 without any array.

exercise.description: Solve four multiplication problems (30×30, 400×8, 15×60, 200×16) and write two division statements for each.

items.prompt: Divide 3005 by 5 using the place-value method. Write the quotient and the remainder. Then write the check: 5 × quotient + remainder = 3005.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Distribute Thousands (3÷5 — insufficient, regroup), Hundreds (30÷5=6), Tens (0÷5=0, write zero), Ones (5÷5=1).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the Th–H–T–O columns on paper and work one place at a time, asking 'How many fives fit?' at each step; stretch: ask what the quotient of 3005 ÷ 5 would become if the dividend were 6010, and why it doubles.

exercise.description: Complete four division problems (7032÷6, 3005÷5, 2874÷14, 9805÷32) using both partial quotient scaffold and place-value (Th–H–T–O) algorithm side by side.

items.prompt: Divide 7056 by 7 using the place-value method. Write the quotient and the remainder, then check your answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Distribute each place: 7÷7=1 Thousand; 0 Hundreds (write 0); 5 Tens ÷ 7 — regroup 56 Ones; 56÷7=8 Ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: work through just the Thousands column together and let the student continue from there; stretch: ask which two digits in the quotient would change, and how, if the dividend were 7063 instead.

items.section_title: Patterns in division and place value
items.prompt: Priya walks 180 km in 20 days. How many kilometres does she walk each day?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Scale: 180 ÷ 20 = 18 ÷ 2 = 9, using the pattern that dividing both dividend and divisor by 10 leaves the quotient unchanged.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: rewrite 180 ÷ 20 as 18 ÷ 2 by crossing a zero from each, then divide; stretch: ask how many days she would need to walk the same total distance if she walked 15 km each day.

exercise.description: Sabina cycles 160 km in 20 days. How many kilometres does she cycle each day?

items.section_title: Patterns in division and place value
items.prompt: Coconuts costing ₹3600 in all are paid for entirely with ₹100 notes. How many ₹100 notes are needed?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total by the note value: 3600 ÷ 100 = 36.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count how many hundreds fit in 3600 using a place value chart; stretch: ask how many ₹50 notes would be needed for the same total.

exercise.description: How many ₹100 notes does Seema need to buy coconuts worth ₹4200?

items.prompt: Use the splitting strategy to find 1260 ÷ 6. Show how you split 1260 into two parts that are easy to divide by 6, then write the final answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the dividend into parts that are multiples of the divisor, divide each part, then add the results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to name the nearest multiple of 6 (in hundreds) that is less than 1260, then find what remains; stretch: ask them to solve the same problem using a subtractive split (1260 = 1320 − 60) and verify both methods agree.

exercise.description: Apply splitting and/or repeated halving strategies to solve: 64÷4, 265÷5, 1560÷8, 4824÷24, 168÷8, 144÷4 using scaffolded diagram frames.

items.section_title: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
items.prompt: A farmer packs 672 coconuts equally into crates of 8. How many full crates does he fill? How many coconuts are left over? Write the check N = D × Q + R.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 672 ÷ 8 = 84 remainder 0. Check: 8 × 84 + 0 = 672. He fills 84 full crates with no coconuts left over.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract batches of 8 (e.g. 8×80=640, remainder 32; 8×4=32, remainder 0) and add partial quotients: 80+4=84.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: begin by asking how many 8s fit in 600 (75) and how many remain, then continue; stretch: ask what happens if 672 coconuts are packed in crates of 9 — how many full crates and how many left over?

exercise.description: Solve eight division problems using partial quotient strategies: 256÷4, 545÷5, 147÷7, 1212÷6, 648÷12, 9648÷48, 775÷25, 796÷4.

items.section_title: Long division using partial quotients and remainder
items.prompt: A school hires buses for a trip. Each bus holds 45 students. There are 378 students going on the trip. How many buses are needed so that all students can travel? Show your division and explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 378 ÷ 45 = 8 remainder 18. Since 18 students remain after filling 8 buses, a 9th bus is needed. Answer: 9 buses.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide to find full buses, then interpret the remainder: if it is non-zero, one extra bus is required.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student how many students 8 buses carry (8×45=360) and how many are still without a seat (378−360=18); stretch: ask the minimum number of students per bus if exactly 8 buses are used, and whether that is possible with buses of fixed capacity 45.

exercise.description: Word problems: oil from 4376 coconuts (4376÷8); theatre samosa packs; buses for 342 students; Sofia's note combinations; picnic cost split; check N=D×Q+R for six division problems (a–f).

items.prompt: A theatre has 475 identical seats arranged in equal rows. Each row has 19 seats. How many full rows are there? Are any seats left ungrouped? Write the division and the check.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 475 ÷ 19 = 25 remainder 0. Check: 19 × 25 + 0 = 475. There are 25 full rows and no seats left ungrouped.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide using place value or partial quotients: 19×20=380, remainder 95; 19×5=95, remainder 0; quotient 25.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start the student with 19×20=380 and ask how many remain; stretch: ask what the seating arrangement would look like if one more row of 19 were added and whether any seats would be ungrouped.

exercise.description: Word problems: theatre shows for 475 people; ice cream per friend; biscuits per person per day; six division problems with remainder check; pattern sets A/B/C; cycle rally distance; identify missing information in 4 problems; bookshelf resource constraint problem.

items.prompt: Munshi Lal sold 6 kg of tomatoes for ₹138 in all. What was the cost of 1 kg of tomatoes? Write the division and the check.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student how much 10 kg would cost if 1 kg costs an estimated ₹20, then adjust; stretch: ask how much 9 kg would cost at ₹23 per kg and whether the total is more or less than ₹200.

exercise.description: Complete Munshi Lal's erased record book: find missing total amounts, quantities, and cost per kg for 4 vegetables using multiplication and division.
